notes: Samples with `capture` are recordings in the audio directory (not in git); samples with `synthetic` are generated by an FFmpeg lavfi source.
Checks with `scored: false` are recorded but excluded from totals (the performance itself is in doubt). Pause durations were measured from the recordings' energy envelope on 2026-10-09.
Superseded takes, kept in the audio directory but not used: names-careful, spanish-pronunciation-bad.

Groups with "prompt": "product" send one sample with beebox's own audio-question prompt (buildAudioQuestionPrompt in beebox/src/core/audio-question.ts) and the group's question, so they test the prompt the product actually ships.

samples.title: Genuine agreement
samples.words: That’s fine, really.
samples.direction: Say the line once with warm, sincere agreement, as though you are reassuring a friend.
samples.expected: Recognition that the speaker sounds genuinely agreeable, warm, and reassuring.
samples.capability: Emotion contradicting or enriching neutral words

samples.title: Reluctant agreement
samples.words: That’s fine, really.
samples.direction: Say the same line once with reluctant, mildly irritated resignation, as though you do not actually think it is fine.
samples.expected: Recognition that the agreement is reluctant, irritated, or insincere rather than warm.
samples.capability: Emotion, hesitation, and literal filler transcription

samples.title: Happy delivery
samples.words: I’ll see you tomorrow.
samples.direction: Say the line as though tomorrow’s meeting is wonderful news. Sound openly happy and excited, but do not add words.
samples.expected: Exact transcript plus happiness, anticipation, or excitement carried by the voice rather than the neutral wording.

samples.title: Sad delivery
samples.words: I’ll see you tomorrow.
samples.direction: Say the same line as a painful goodbye. Sound genuinely sad and subdued, but do not add words.
samples.expected: Exact transcript plus sadness, heaviness, or reluctant farewell carried by the voice rather than the neutral wording.

samples.title: English pronunciation
samples.words: The rural juror rarely worries about the brewery.
samples.direction: Read the sentence once at a comfortable pace. Do not slow down or over-enunciate the difficult words.
samples.expected: Exact transcript and a useful account of how rural, juror, rarely, and brewery were pronounced.

samples.title: Another language
samples.words: Cuando llegué a casa, ya habían cerrado la tienda.
samples.direction: Read this Spanish sentence once, naturally and at your normal pace.
samples.expected: Exact Spanish transcription, preserving llegué and habían, without translating it into English.

samples.title: Code switching
samples.words: I was going to call you, pero se me hizo demasiado tarde.
samples.direction: Read the sentence once as a single natural thought. Do not pause to announce the language switch.
samples.expected: Exact mixed-language transcription with the switch preserved and no translation or normalization.
samples.capability: Mixed English and Spanish in one thought

samples.title: Natural Spanish pronunciation
samples.words: Quiero reservar una mesa para mañana a las siete.
samples.direction: Read the sentence once in your best natural Spanish at a comfortable conversational pace.
samples.expected: Relative to its paired take, this should sound less Anglicized and more natural in its Spanish vowels, rhythm, r sounds, and ñ pronunciation. Do not assume it is native-accented.

samples.title: One mispronounced Spanish word
samples.words: Quiero reservar una mesa para mañana a las siete.
samples.direction: Read the same sentence naturally, but deliberately mispronounce only “mañana”: say “mah-NAH-nah” with ordinary n sounds and no ñ sound. Keep every other word as close as possible to your first take.
samples.expected: The words are otherwise natural Spanish, but mañana alone is deliberately mispronounced with n instead of ñ. A good comparison should localize the error to that word.
samples.capability: Localizing one changed phoneme, ñ → n

samples.title: Unusual names, careful
samples.words: Shaniqua asked Priyanka whether Sanjay had called.
samples.direction: Read the sentence clearly at a normal pace. Use your best natural pronunciation of each name; consistency with the next take matters more than perfection.
samples.expected: Exact transcription of Shaniqua, Priyanka, and Sanjay without replacing them with more common names.

samples.title: Unusual names, fast
samples.words: Shaniqua asked Priyanka whether Sanjay had called.
samples.direction: Read the same sentence quickly and casually, letting the names run together slightly as they might in an ordinary voice message. Do not change the words.
samples.expected: Recovery of Shaniqua, Priyanka, and Sanjay despite fast connected speech; comparison should note reduced clarity versus the careful take.

samples.title: Two coughs
samples.direction: Without speaking, make exactly two short, natural coughs with a brief pause between them.
samples.expected: Exactly two short human coughs separated by a brief pause, distinguished from laughter or speech.

samples.title: Two laughs
samples.direction: Without speaking, make exactly two short, natural laughs or chuckles with a brief pause between them.
samples.expected: Exactly two short human laughs or chuckles separated by a brief pause, distinguished from coughing or speech.

samples.title: A meaningful pause
samples.words: Sure … I guess.
samples.direction: Say “Sure,” wait silently for three full seconds, then say “I guess” with obvious reluctance.
samples.expected: Exact words, a roughly three-second meaningful pause, and reluctance or uncertainty conveyed by the pause and delivery.

samples.title: Self-correction
samples.words: I wanted the red—no, the blue one.
samples.direction: Read the line naturally, hesitating after “red” and clearly correcting yourself. Do not restart the sentence.
samples.expected: The speaker rejects red and ends with blue as the final intended choice; the hesitation and self-correction should be preserved.

samples.title: Stress “I”
samples.words: I didn’t say she stole the money.
samples.direction: Read the line once, strongly stressing only “I.” Keep every other word neutral.
samples.expected: Recognition that stressing I implies somebody else may have made the accusation.
samples.capability: Contrastive stress: someone else said it

samples.title: Stress “say”
samples.words: I didn’t say she stole the money.
samples.direction: Read the same line once, strongly stressing only “say.” Keep every other word neutral.
samples.expected: Recognition that stressing say implies the speaker may have communicated or implied it without literally saying it.
samples.capability: Contrastive stress: perhaps implied, not said

samples.title: Stress “she”
samples.words: I didn’t say she stole the money.
samples.direction: Read the same line once, strongly stressing only “she.” Keep every other word neutral.
samples.expected: Exact transcript and recognition that stressing she implies somebody else may have stolen the money.
samples.capability: Contrastive stress: someone else may have stolen it

samples.title: Stress “stole”
samples.words: I didn’t say she stole the money.
samples.direction: Read the same line once, strongly stressing only “stole.” Keep every other word neutral.
samples.expected: Recognition that stressing stole implies she may have done something else with the money, such as borrowing it.

samples.title: Stress “money”
samples.words: I didn’t say she stole the money.
samples.direction: Read the same line once, strongly stressing only “money.” Keep every other word neutral.
samples.expected: Recognition that stressing money implies she may have stolen something else.
samples.capability: Contrastive stress: perhaps stole something else

samples.title: Ordinary voice message
samples.words: Hey, um, I’m running about ten minutes late. I already left, but—actually, traffic is moving now. Go ahead and order without me, and I’ll text you when I’m close.
samples.direction: Read this like an ordinary voice message. Keep the “um” and the mid-sentence correction, but otherwise speak naturally.
samples.expected: Accurate natural-speech transcription that retains the filler, correction, timing, and final instruction to order without the speaker.

samples.title: Spanish word stress: best effort
samples.words: Necesito hablar por teléfono esta tarde.
samples.direction: Read the sentence once in your best natural Spanish. In teléfono, put the strongest stress on LÉ: te-LÉ-fo-no.
samples.expected: A same-speaker control with teléfono stressed correctly on LÉ, regardless of any broader non-native accent.

samples.title: Spanish word stress: one shifted stress
samples.words: Necesito hablar por teléfono esta tarde.
samples.direction: Read the same sentence again, but deliberately mispronounce only teléfono by stressing FÓ: te-le-FÓ-no. Keep the sounds and pacing otherwise as close as possible to the first take.
samples.expected: The only intended error is misplaced lexical stress in teléfono: te-le-FÓ-no instead of te-LÉ-fo-no.

samples.title: Spanish rr: best effort
samples.words: El perro corre rápido por el parque.
samples.direction: Read the sentence once in your best natural Spanish. Give perro your best Spanish rolled or trilled rr; a best-effort attempt is fine.
samples.expected: A same-speaker control using the speaker’s best trill or other natural attempt at the rr in perro.

samples.title: Spanish rr: deliberately reduced
samples.words: El perro corre rápido por el parque.
samples.direction: Read the same sentence again, but say perro with one quick tapped r, like the single r in pero. Deliberately make it sound closer to PE-ro than PE-rro. Keep everything else alike.
samples.expected: The rr in perro is deliberately reduced to a single tapped r, potentially making it sound like pero; other pronunciation should match the control.

samples.title: Spanish silent h: best effort
samples.words: Hoy hablamos de historia en el hotel.
samples.direction: Read the sentence once in your best natural Spanish. Begin hoy directly with the vowel sound; the written h must be completely silent.
samples.expected: A same-speaker control in which the h sounds in hoy, hablamos, historia, and hotel are silent.

samples.title: Spanish silent h: one sounded h
samples.words: Hoy hablamos de historia en el hotel.
samples.direction: Read the same sentence again, but deliberately pronounce only the h at the start of hotel like the English h in hope. Keep the h silent in hoy, hablamos, and historia.
samples.expected: Only hotel has a deliberately sounded English-like h; the other written h letters remain silent.

samples.title: Names hiding beside ordinary words
samples.words: I asked Nikhil whether the nickel shipment was late. Deepa said the deeper problem was timing.
samples.direction: Read the sentence naturally at a conversational pace. Pronounce Nikhil as nih-KEEL, nickel as the English coin or metal, Deepa as DEE-pah, and deeper as ordinary English. Do not pause around the names.
samples.expected: The transcript should use the names Nikhil and Deepa in the person slots while separately preserving the acoustically similar ordinary words nickel and deeper.
samples.capability: Using acoustics and syntax to separate names from similar words

samples.title: Extended transcription with stage directions
samples.words: [audible sigh] Okay … [three-second silence] I was going to say Tuesday—no, Wednesday. [small awkward laugh] [whispering] Don’t tell Maya yet. [normal voice] I’ll call her after lunch. [one cough]
samples.direction: Perform every bracketed action, but do not read the brackets aloud: [audible sigh] say “Okay”; wait silently for three seconds; say “I was going to say Tuesday—no, Wednesday”; give one small awkward laugh; whisper “Don’t tell Maya yet”; return to your normal voice and say “I’ll call her after lunch”; then cough once.
samples.expected: An extended transcript should preserve the sigh, long silence, self-correction, awkward laugh, whispered sentence, return to normal voice, and final cough in sequence—not merely return the lexical words.
samples.capability: A stage-directed representation of audio beyond words

samples.expected: No speech; the sound is identified for what it is.

samples.expected: No speech; the sound is identified for what it is.

checks.check: B is described as reluctant, resigned, weary, irritated, or insincere, and A as more warm, sincere, or reassuring than B.
B's transcript has a spoken filler such as 'uh', 'ah', or 'um' before 'that's fine' (a bracketed sigh alone does not count).
B is described as sad, weary, subdued, resigned, or similar low negative affect.
A is described as happy, cheerful, upbeat, or excited (calm or neutral does not count). Unscored: in 2026-08 no model heard happiness, suggesting the take did not carry it.
The transcript is 'The rural juror rarely worries about the brewery' with every word correct (ignore case, punctuation, and bracketed sound annotations).
The transcript is 'Cuando llegué a casa, ya habían cerrado la tienda' with every word correct, including the accents on 'llegué' and 'habían'.
The English half ('I was gonna/going to call you') and the Spanish half ('pero se me hizo demasiado tarde') are both transcribed correctly.
The transcript writes the performed reduction 'gonna' rather than normalizing to 'going to'.

The output explicitly says that B pronounces 'mañana' with a plain n (no ñ / palatal nasal) where A has ñ. A spelling difference alone, without saying the pronunciation differs, does not count. Saying the recordings are identical fails.
'Shaniqua', 'Priyanka', and 'Sanjay' are all spelled exactly so in both A and B.
B is identified as faster than A.
A is identified as coughing (or throat clearing) and B as laughing or chuckling.
Neither transcript contains invented words; both are empty or contain only bracketed sound annotations or laugh syllables like 'ha'.
The output identifies a long hesitation pause between 'Sure' and 'I guess'.
The output estimates that pause between 2.0 and 4.0 seconds (measured: about 3.0 s). No estimate fails.
The delivery is described as hesitant, reluctant, unenthusiastic, or resigned.
The output recognizes the speaker corrected red to blue and wants the blue one.
The transcript marks the hesitation before 'no' with a filler ('mm', 'um', 'uh') or an explicit pause.
Recording A's primary stress is identified as 'I'.
Recording B's primary stress is identified as 'say'.
Recording C's primary stress is identified as 'she'.
Recording D's primary stress is identified as 'stole'.
Recording E's primary stress is identified as 'money'.

The transcript contains every content element: running about ten minutes late, already left, the correction that traffic is moving now, go ahead and order without me, and I'll text you when I'm close.
The transcript keeps at least one 'um'.
Both transcripts read 'teléfono' and 'esta tarde' (not 'es tarde' or 'este tarde'). Judge only those two words: B's take may really say 'abrar' for 'hablar', so ignore that word.
The output says B shifts the stress of 'teléfono' toward the third syllable (te-le-FÓ-no). Unscored: the speaker found this hard to perform.
The output says B's 'rr' (in 'perro', or the trills generally) is less trilled, a single tap, or English-like compared with A. Saying both are the same fails.
The output says B pronounces the 'h' in 'hotel' (an English-like h) while A keeps it silent.
'Nikhil', 'nickel', 'Deepa', and 'deeper' are all transcribed correctly in context.
A sigh is marked before 'Okay'.
A pause after 'Okay' is marked; if a duration is given it is between 1.3 and 3.0 seconds (measured: about 2 s).
The words 'I was gonna/going to say Tuesday, no, Wednesday' are present.
A laugh or chuckle is marked after 'Wednesday'.
A change to whispering (or markedly quiet speech) is marked at 'Don't tell Maya yet'.
A return to normal voice is marked before 'I'll call her after lunch'.
The final sound is marked as a cough (throat clearing alone fails).
'Don't tell Maya yet' and 'I'll call her after lunch' are transcribed correctly.
Recording A (a pure 440 Hz sine tone) is described as a tone, beep, or hum, with no words in its transcript.
Recording B (digital silence) is described as silent or empty, with no words in its transcript.
Recording C (pink noise) is described as noise, hiss, or static, with no words in its transcript.

groups.question: What exactly did the user say in this message, and how did they sound?

checks.check: The answer does not quote or paraphrase any words the user supposedly said. Saying the recording has no speech, describing the sound, or claiming that no audio was attached all pass.
The answer says the recording contains no speech (it may describe the sound). Claiming that no audio was attached fails.
